title: Images, Fonts & CSS Performance
objectives: Serve responsive images in modern formats without layout shift
Pick font-display and preload strategies that avoid invisible text
Explain why CSS blocks rendering and what critical CSS buys
Judge selector cost claims with measurements, not folklore
body: Images are usually the heaviest bytes on a page, fonts can hold text hostage, and stylesheets block first paint. These three resource types decide whether the page looks fast, and each has one dominant mistake worth unlearning. ## The problem Your marketing page ships a 2 MB hero JPEG at desktop resolution even on phones, a web font that leaves headings blank for two seconds, and 300 KB of CSS — 80% of it unused. LCP and CLS are both poor and nobody knows which fix matters most. ## Constraints - LCP is usually an image: its size, format and discovery timing cap your best possible score. - An `` without `width`/`height` (or CSS aspect-ratio) reserves no space, so late images push content down — that is CLS. - Web fonts with `font-display: block` cause FOIT (invisible text); `swap` causes FOUT (fallback flash) — text shows either late or twice. - Stylesheets in `` block rendering: the browser will not paint until CSS arrives and is parsed. - Selector matching is fast in modern engines; the real CSS costs are file size and render-blocking, not `.a .b .c` vs `.a-b`. ## Options ```html ``` Below-fold images get `loading="lazy"`; above-fold LCP images get `fetchpriority="high"` and are *not* lazy. ## Tradeoffs AVIF/WebP cut image bytes 30–60% but need a JPEG/PNG fallback for old browsers (the `` element handles that). `font-display: swap` shows text immediately but risks a visible re-layout when the real font has different metrics — mitigated with `size-adjust` metric overrides. Inlining critical CSS speeds first paint but doubles maintenance and can inline bytes for routes the user never visits. ## Decision Convert images to AVIF/WebP with fallbacks, always set intrinsic dimensions, lazy-load below the fold only. Preload the one or two fonts used above the fold with `font-display: swap`. Inline only the small critical CSS for the landing route; defer the rest. Ignore selector micro-optimizations until a style-recalc trace proves they matter. ## Measure it Check LCP element and CLS sources in the Performance panel or Lighthouse; compare image bytes before/after format changes with the Network panel. For fonts, record whether text paints before `load` fires. For CSS, use Coverage to size the unused portion. Every change gets a before/after run on the same URL and device class. ## Best practices - Set `width` and `height` (or aspect-ratio) on every image to reserve layout space. - Serve AVIF or WebP with a `` fallback; never lazy-load the LCP image. - Preload above-fold fonts and pair with `font-display: swap` plus `size-adjust` metrics. - Keep render-blocking CSS small; defer or split the rest per route. - Treat selector performance claims as hypotheses to profile, not rules to obey. ## Common mistakes - Lazy-loading the hero image and tanking LCP to save bandwidth the user needed anyway. - Using `font-display: block` on body text and shipping a second of invisible content. - Shipping 2× PNG screenshots as content images because it is what the designer exported. - Rewriting selectors for speed based on a 2013 blog post, without a style-recalc measurement. - Adding `preload` for five fonts and delaying the actual critical requests.

exercise.prompt: Analyze three resource decisions and render a verdict for each: (1) an image config — verdict must flag missing dimensions as CLS risk and non-modern formats as byte waste; (2) a font config — flag font-display block as FOIT risk and praise swap; (3) a stylesheet — flag over 100 KB unsplit CSS as render-blocking. Implement the two missing verdict functions.
hints: Build strings from conditions: dimensions first, then format, then LCP handling.
font-display: block hides text while the font loads — that is the FOIT definition.
Reuse the comparison style of cssVerdict: conditions joined into one sentence.

questions.prompt: An image without width/height attributes loads late. What user-visible symptom follows?
options: The page stays blank until the image arrives
Content below the image jumps down when it arrives (layout shift)
The image renders at full viewport width regardless of CSS
The browser blocks JavaScript until the image is decoded
questions.explanation: Without intrinsic dimensions the browser cannot reserve space before the image loads, so late arrival pushes content down — the classic CLS failure.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between FOIT and FOUT?
options: FOIT hides text while the web font loads; FOUT shows a fallback font first
FOIT blocks images; FOUT blocks CSS
FOIT only happens with system fonts; FOUT only with web fonts
They are two names for the same behavior
questions.explanation: font-display: block causes Flash Of Invisible Text; swap causes Flash Of Unstyled Text where the fallback font is replaced once the web font arrives.
